Q: Error while flashing linux on STM32MP1 board A:

I had that issue lot of times, check your FlashLayout file, the STM32_CubeProgrammer timeouts waiting for the U-boot's stm32prog command deleting and earsing partitions marked with PED in the FlashLayout file.

If that is the case, just run the STM32_CubeProgrammer flashing command again and it will pass, otherwise, you can post your FlashLayout and/or the serial log and then I 'll update the answer accordingly

Q: Using std::launder to retrieve a dynamic array A:

<disclaimer> This is not a proper answer but a large comment (no permitted by SO interface), motivated by comments to the original question (thanks to Ted Lyngmo and Davis Herring). It may become a proper answer or may be disproved and removed accordingly. </disclaimer>.

A plausible interpretation could have been that a T* is always an array address, as soon as it is the memory location of a T object (https://eel.is/c++draft/dcl.array#6 and https://eel.is/c++draft/expr.new#11).

An object of type “array of N U” consists of a contiguously allocated non-empty set of N subobjects of type U, known as the elements of the array, and numbered 0 to N-1. The element numbered 0 is termed the first element of the array.

and

When the allocated type is “array of N T” (that is, the noptr-new-declarator syntax is used or the new-type-id or type-id denotes an array type), the new-expression yields a prvalue of type “pointer to T” that points to the initial element (if any) of the array. Otherwise, let T be the allocated type; the new-expression is a prvalue of type “pointer to T” that points to the object created.

If there is a single T object, it is by all means equivalent to an array of size 1 (https://eel.is/c++draft/basic.compound#3).

...an object of type T that is not an array element is considered to belong to an array with one element of type T

Then the size can be known only at runtime, the array could have been created implicitly, from a new expression or an array declaration, it does not matter.

Thus when returning a T* from std::launder, and performing pointer arithmetic (https://eel.is/c++draft/expr.add#4), the compiler must assume that it is correct has soon as we point at most to the "one past end" element. Similarly, dereferencing an array element (either by *(ptr+i) or ptr[i]), the compiler must assume that there is a living T object there. If this assumptions are not true, the behavior is undefined.

The point I am the most unsure of is that array can be implicitly created, while there objects are not (typically if they are not of implicit lifetime type): does this analysis hold when an array is in its lifetime but not its elements? should we interpret https://eel.is/c++draft/dcl.array#6 more liberally accepting such arrays?
